usage: Count small candies with 하나/한 개; 하나 is the natural default at a counter.
까다 is the verb for peeling off a wrapper — never 열다 (open) for candy.
막대(stick) + 사탕, a fixed compound written as one word.
to hold a candy in one's mouth
물다 (to hold in the mouth) fits hard candy you suck on, not chew.
examples: 사탕 좋아해요?
Do you like candy?
Drop the subject in casual talk; context supplies 'you'.
편의점에서 사탕 한 봉지 샀어요.
I bought a bag of candy at the convenience store.
봉지 is the counter for a bag/packet of snacks.
목 아플 때 사탕 하나 입에 물고 있으면 좀 나아요.
When my throat hurts, keeping a candy in my mouth helps a bit.
Throat-soothing candy is treated as a mild everyday remedy; 물고 있다 = keep held in the mouth.
nuance: 사탕 means hard, sugar-based candy and lollipops — the kind you suck, not the chewy gummies (those are strictly 젤리) or 초콜릿. It is Sino-Korean, 砂糖 'sand-sugar' (the same 糖 'sugar' element in 설탕 table sugar and 당분 sugar content), which is why it sits in the sweets family rather than being a generic 'sweet treat'. Register is fully neutral: a child or an adult says it the same way. The pitfall for English speakers is the verb: you do not 열다 (open) a candy, you 까다 (peel/unwrap) it, and you 물다 or 빨다 (hold/suck) rather than 먹다 when sucking it. Seasonally it carries a faint romance: on White Day (3/14) men give 사탕 to answer the 초콜릿 women give on Valentine's Day.

mistakes: Calling gummy candies 사탕 — soft chewy ones are 젤리, a separate category Koreans never merge with 사탕.
Saying 사탕을 열다 for 'unwrap a candy'; the correct verb is 사탕을 까다.
Using 먹다 for sucking a hard candy — when it stays in the mouth, 물다/빨다 is more accurate than 먹다.

usage: 개 counts a single piece; a whole bar is 한 판.
녹다 (to melt) is the verb you hear in summer or in a warm hand.
Loanword modifiers 다크/밀크/화이트 sit directly before 초콜릿.
줄이다 = to reduce; standard health-talk phrasing.
examples: 초콜릿 좋아해요?
Do you like chocolate?
Plain everyday question; subject dropped.
피곤할 때 초콜릿 먹으면 기분이 좀 좋아져요.
When I'm tired, eating chocolate lifts my mood a bit.
기분이 좋아지다 = one's mood improves; -아지다 marks the gradual change.
밸런타인데이에 좋아하는 사람한테 초콜릿 주려고 직접 만들었어요.
I made chocolate by hand to give to my crush on Valentine's Day.
Handmade (직접 만든) 초콜릿 on Feb 14 is the big Korean custom; 주려고 = intending to give.
nuance: 초콜릿 is a direct loanword from English 'chocolate', and the single most important thing to learn is the spelling: 초콜릿 is standard, while 초콜렛 is a widespread misspelling even among natives — write the former. Unlike the native-word sweets here, it takes loanword flavor modifiers (다크/밀크/화이트) placed before it. Counting trips people up: a flat bar is counted with 판 (한 판), individual squares or wrapped pieces with 개 (한 개), so 'one chocolate' is ambiguous until you pick the counter that matches the shape. Culturally it is the default Valentine's gift from women to men, mirrored by 사탕 on White Day. Pitfall: English lets 'chocolate' be a mass noun ('some chocolate'), but in Korean you still attach a counter, so 초콜릿 좀 (some) or 초콜릿 한 개 (one piece) rather than a bare count.

mistakes: Writing 초콜렛 instead of the standard 초콜릿 — the second is correct even though both are heard.
Using 판 for a single square — a whole bar is 한 판, one piece is 한 개.
Treating it as an uncountable mass like English 'chocolate'; Korean still needs a counter, e.g. 초콜릿 한 조각/한 개.

usage: Sold by the 봉지 at convenience stores.
곰(bear) + 젤리; by far the most popular type.
쫄깃하다 describes the springy chew people love in 젤리.
씹다 (to chew) suits 젤리 — unlike hard 사탕, which you suck.
examples: 젤리 더 먹어도 돼?
Can I have more gummies?
Casual permission: -아/어도 돼요? shortened to 돼?
젤리는 충치 생기기 쉬우니까 조금만 먹어.
Gummies cause cavities easily, so eat just a little.
생기기 쉽다 = easy to develop; 조금만 = just a little.
요즘 편의점엔 마라맛 젤리 같은 신기한 맛까지 있어서 한참 골랐어요.
These days convenience stores even have novelty flavors like mala gummies, so I spent ages choosing.
마라맛 is a recent trend; 신기하다 = novel; 한참 = a good while; 고르다 = to pick.
nuance: 젤리 (a loanword from English 'jelly') is the catch-all for chewy gummy sweets — gummy bears, fruit gummies, sour gummies — and is firmly a separate category from hard 사탕 and from 초콜릿; Koreans never file 젤리 under 사탕. The word can also name a wobbly dessert jelly, but in everyday snack talk it almost always means gummies. The defining texture word is 쫄깃하다/쫀득하다 (springy-chewy), and the natural verb is 씹다 (chew), contrasting with the 빨다/물다 (suck) you use for 사탕. The classic English-speaker trap is confusing 젤리 with 잼 (jam, the bread spread) because both come from 'jelly/jam' — they are completely different foods. Convenience stores carry an enormous, constantly rotating gummy wall, so 젤리 is genuinely high-frequency vocabulary.

Using 빨다/물다 (suck) with 젤리 — gummies are chewed, so the verb is 씹다.

usage: 봉지 is the go-to counter for bagged snacks.
부스러기 = crumbs; handy when cleaning up.
눅눅하다 describes chips that lost their crunch; opposite of 바삭하다.
to tear open the snack bag
뜯다 (to tear) is how you open a sealed 과자 봉지.
examples: 과자 사러 갈래?
Wanna go buy some snacks?
-(으)러 가다 = go in order to do; 갈래? is a casual invite.
영화 볼 때 과자랑 음료수는 필수예요.
Snacks and a drink are a must when watching a movie.
필수예요 = it's essential; 랑 links the pair casually.
이 과자는 봉지를 뜯으면 생각보다 절반이 공기예요.
When you open this snack bag, half of it is air, more than you'd expect.
A common joke about 질소과자 (nitrogen-filled bags); 뜯다 = to tear open.
nuance: 과자 is Sino-Korean, 菓子 (菓 'confection/fruit' + 子 a noun suffix), and works as the umbrella term for crunchy packaged snacks — chips, crackers, biscuits, corn puffs, basically the salty-or-sweet bagged stuff in the snack aisle. It deliberately excludes the other categories on this list: gummies are 젤리, hard candy is 사탕, chocolate is 초콜릿. The boundary that trips learners is 과자 vs 쿠키: a freshly baked café cookie is 쿠키, while 과자 leans toward mass-produced, packaged snacks, so calling an artisan cookie 과자 sounds slightly off. Counting is by 봉지 (bag), not by piece, because these come bagged; you 뜯다 (tear) the bag open. Texture is 바삭하다 (crispy) when fresh, 눅눅하다 (soggy) when stale. Koreans love joking about 질소과자 — bags that feel mostly full of nitrogen gas rather than chips.

mistakes: Using 과자 for a bakery/café cookie you'd call 쿠키 — 과자 implies packaged, mass-market snacks.
Counting bagged snacks by piece; the natural counter is 봉지 (한 봉지).
Lumping 사탕/젤리/초콜릿 under 과자 — 과자 is the crunchy salty/biscuit category, not candy.

usage: 통 (tub/bucket) is the cinema counter for popcorn.
Flavor sits before 팝콘; 카라멜/치즈 are the most common.
튀기다 (to pop/fry) is the standard verb for making it.
Cinemas let you split two flavors; 반반 = half-half.
examples: 집에서 전자레인지 팝콘 돌려 먹었어요.
I made microwave popcorn at home.
돌리다 = to run (the microwave); home popcorn comes by the 봉지.
영화관에서 팝콘 큰 거 하나 시켰어요.
I ordered one large popcorn at the cinema.
큰 거 = the big one; 시키다 = to order.
고소한 팝콘 냄새 때문에 안 사고는 못 배겨요.
The savory popcorn smell makes it impossible not to buy some.
고소하다 = nutty-savory; idiomatic 못 배기다 = can't resist.
nuance: 팝콘 is a loanword from English 'popcorn' and in Korea is strongly bound to the cinema: the defaults are 카라멜 (caramel) and 치즈 (cheese), often ordered 반반 (half-and-half) and bundled with a drink as a 콤보 set. This is a key culture point — plain buttered popcorn is the mental default in English, but in Korea sweet/cheese flavors dominate, so just saying 팝콘 at a 영화관 may get you a flavored tub. Counters differ by context: the cinema tub is 통 (한 통), while microwave popcorn at home is counted by 봉지. The smell word is the classic 고소하다 (the warm, nutty, slightly savory aroma), a flavor adjective with no neat English equivalent. The verb to make it is 튀기다 (pop/fry), the same verb behind 튀김.

mistakes: Ordering popcorn by 개 — at a cinema you ask for 한 통 (one tub).

Describing the smell as 맛있는 냄새 only — the precise word Koreans use is 고소하다.

usage: Count with 개; 하나 is the easy default at a stall.
씨앗(seeds) + 호떡, a popular nut-and-seed version from Busan.
굽다 here means griddle/pan-fry, not bake; it is a ㅂ-irregular (구워요).
The molten sugar filling is famously scalding; warn 천천히 먹어.
examples: 호떡 두 개요.
Two hotteok, please.
At a busy stall, drop the verb; 개 + 요 is enough to order.
겨울에 길거리에서 따뜻한 호떡 먹는 게 최고예요.
Eating warm hotteok on the street in winter is the best.
Quintessential winter street food; -는 게 최고예요 = ...is the best.
호떡 한 입 베어 물자마자 흑설탕이 흘러나와서 입천장을 데었어요.
The moment I bit into the hotteok, the brown sugar oozed out and I burned the roof of my mouth.
베어 물다 = to bite into; -자마자 = as soon as; 흑설탕 = brown sugar.
nuance: 호떡 is a chewy, griddle-fried wheat-flour pancake with a molten brown-sugar-and-cinnamon center, sold piping hot from winter street carts. The 호 in 호떡 is the 한자 胡, historically 'foreign/Chinese', marking its origin as an introduced food, attached to native 떡 — but here is the crucial distinction: although the name ends in 떡, 호떡 is NOT a rice cake. Real 떡 is made from pounded rice; 호떡 is a flour dough that is pan-fried, so do not assume the texture or ingredients of 떡. The second pitfall is taste: English speakers often expect a savory pancake, but the classic filling is sweet brown sugar (savory 야채 호떡 exists but is the exception). The verb is 굽다 (griddle), a ㅂ-irregular giving 구워요. The filling is dangerously hot, so locals genuinely warn 천천히 먹어 (eat slowly); trendy 씨앗 호떡 stuffed with seeds and nuts is a market favorite, famously around Busan's BIFF square.

usage: Sold by count (개); often cheaper as a 묶음 (bundle).
슈크림 fillings now rival the classic 팥(red bean).
the red bean is packed all the way to the tail
꽉 차다 = packed full; locals judge a stall by this.
examples: 붕어빵 머리부터 먹어, 꼬리부터 먹어?
Do you eat bungeoppang head-first or tail-first?
A playful national debate; 머리부터 = starting from the head.
요즘은 붕어빵 파는 데 찾기가 힘들어요.
These days it's hard to find a place selling bungeoppang.
Stalls have grown scarce; -기가 힘들다 = it's hard to...
추운 날 갓 구운 붕어빵을 봉지째 들고 호호 불면서 먹었어요.
On a cold day I ate freshly griddled bungeoppang straight from the bag, blowing on it to cool it.
갓 구운 = just griddled; 봉지째 = bag and all; 호호 불다 = to blow to cool.
nuance: 붕어빵 is a fish-shaped pastry of waffle-like batter filled with sweet red-bean paste, the iconic Korean winter street snack that pairs with 호떡 and 군고구마. The name is 붕어 (crucian carp) + 빵 (bread, itself a loanword via Portuguese pão), and the single biggest trap for English speakers is taking the fish part literally: 붕어빵 contains no fish whatsoever — it is named purely for the fish-shaped mold. Because of that shape, learners reach for the animal counter 마리, but pastries take 개 (세 개), never 마리. The classic filling is 팥 (red bean); 슈크림 (custard) and even pizza versions now compete. Figuratively, 붕어빵 also means 'identical/spitting image' (e.g. 붕어빵처럼 똑같다) because they all come out of the same mold. Stalls have become rare enough that fans share locations via a 붕어빵 지도 app, and people fondly argue over eating head-first vs. tail-first.

usage: Sold by the piece (개) or by weight.
the roasted sweet potato is warm
Warmth is the whole appeal in winter; ask 따뜻해요?
to peel the skin off and eat
꿀(honey) + 고구마: the extra-sweet, moist variety people request.
examples: 겨울 되니까 군고구마 생각이 간절해요.
Now that it's winter, I really crave roasted sweet potato.
생각이 간절하다 = to crave intensely; -니까 = now that/because.
요즘은 편의점에서도 군고구마를 팔더라고요.
These days they even sell roasted sweet potatoes at convenience stores.
-더라고요 reports a mildly surprising thing you observed.
군고구마는 호일에 싸여 있어서 손이 안 뜨거워서 좋아요.
Roasted sweet potato comes wrapped in foil, so your hands don't get hot — I like that.
호일에 싸이다 = to be wrapped in foil; -아서 chains reason to result.
nuance: 군고구마 is a fixed compound, 군 (the past-modifier of 굽다, 'roasted/grilled') + 고구마 (sweet potato), so it literally means 'roasted sweet potato' — and that frozen form matters: when ordering you say the one word 군고구마, not the spelled-out 구운 고구마, which sounds like a description rather than the named street snack. It's a beloved winter food traditionally sold from a barrel-drum roaster on a cart, now also stocked warm at convenience stores, completing the winter trio with 호떡 and 붕어빵. The key vocabulary contrast for learners is 고구마 (sweet potato) vs 감자 (potato): they are different vegetables, and mixing them up changes the dish entirely. People prize the 꿀고구마 variety for its sticky, honey-like sweetness. (Note that 고구마 also has a slang sense — a frustrating, stifling situation — but 군고구마 stays literal.)

usage: Sold by 인분 (portion) at 분식 stalls, not by the piece.
to dip it in salt to eat
찍다 = to dip; many eat 순대 with plain salt.
Do you eat the organ meats too?
내장 (liver, lung) comes mixed in; some skip it.
to dip the sundae in tteokbokki sauce
A classic 분식 move; 국물 = the broth/sauce.
examples: 분식집에서 순대랑 튀김 같이 시켰어요.
I ordered sundae and fritters together at the snack shop.
분식집 = snack/street-food shop; 같이 시키다 = order together.
순대는 소금이랑 먹을지 양념장이랑 먹을지 늘 고민돼요.
I always agonize over eating sundae with salt or with seasoned sauce.
-(으)ㄹ지 ...-(으)ㄹ지 = whether to do A or B; regional tastes differ.
속초 가면 일반 순대보다 훨씬 큰 아바이순대를 꼭 먹어 봐요.
When I go to Sokcho I always try abai-sundae, which is much bigger than regular sundae.
아바이순대 is a famous Sokcho specialty; -아 보다 = try doing.
nuance: 순대 is a steamed sausage made from pig intestine stuffed with 당면 (glass noodles), blood, and other fillings — a pillar of 분식 (snack-shop) culture alongside 떡볶이 and 튀김. The first thing for an English speaker to lock in is the false friend: the English dessert 'sundae' (ice cream) is completely unrelated; that is 선데이 or just 아이스크림 in Korean, while 순대 is a savory blood sausage. The nearest savory cousin is 소시지 (Western sausage), but 순대 is its own traditional category, not a type of 소시지. There is a genuine regional split — some dip it in plain 소금 (salt), others in 양념장 (seasoned sauce) — and it is sold by 인분 (portion), not by 개. The organ meats (내장) usually come on the side, and ordering without them is fine. A famous regional kind is 아바이순대 from Sokcho.

usage: 꼬치 = skewer; the street form is folded onto a stick.
The hot 국물 (broth) is free and beloved in winter.
오뎅 is the very common colloquial (Japanese-origin) term.
셀프 = self-service; refill your own paper cup for free.
examples: 어묵 꼬치 다섯 개 먹고 국물도 두 컵 마셨어요.
I ate five fish-cake skewers and drank two cups of broth too.
Count 꼬치 (skewers) and 컵 (cups); 도 = also.
추운 날 포장마차에서 어묵 국물 마시면 몸이 녹아요.
Drinking fish-cake broth at a street tent on a cold day warms you right up.
포장마차 = street food tent; 몸이 녹다 = to thaw/warm up.
부산 어묵이 워낙 유명해서 갈 때마다 선물로 사 와요.
Busan fish cake is so famous that I buy some as a gift every time I go.
워낙 = (so) by nature/famously; -ㄹ 때마다 = every time.
nuance: 어묵 is the standard word for fish cake — ground fish paste shaped and cooked — and the register issue is the heart of this entry. In everyday speech most people, including at stalls, casually say 오뎅 (from Japanese おでん); 어묵 is the 'proper', recommended-Korean term you should default to in writing and polite contexts, while recognizing 오뎅 when you hear it. The 한자 is 魚 'fish' (어) + native 묵 (a set jelly/curd, as in 도토리묵 acorn jelly), so the word literally frames it as a 'fish curd'. The street form is folded onto a skewer (꼬치) and comes with an endlessly refilled, free hot 국물 in winter — and that broth is 셀프 (self-serve), so you do not pay per cup, a frequent point of confusion for visitors. Busan (부산어묵) is the celebrated home of it, and packaged 어묵 is both a soup ingredient and a common gift.

usage: 모둠 = an assortment of mixed pieces.
Ingredient + 튀김 names each fritter; 오징어/새우/고구마.
바삭하다 = crispy, the key quality marker; opposite 눅눅하다.
to dip the fritters in tteokbokki sauce
The quintessential 분식 way to eat them.
examples: 분식집에서 튀김이랑 순대 시켜서 나눠 먹었어요.
We ordered fritters and sundae at the snack shop and shared.
나눠 먹다 = to share food; -아서 chains the actions.
갓 튀긴 튀김이 제일 바삭하고 맛있어요.
Freshly fried fritters are the crispiest and tastiest.
갓 튀긴 = just-fried; note 튀긴 (verb) modifying 튀김 (noun).
김말이 튀김은 겉은 바삭한데 안에 당면이 가득 들어 있어요.
Gimmari fritters are crispy outside but packed with glass noodles inside.
김말이 = seaweed-rolled fritter; -는데 contrasts outside vs inside.
nuance: 튀김 is a native noun built from the verb 튀기다 (to deep-fry) plus the nominalizing -ㅁ, literally 'a frying / a fried thing', and it means battered deep-fried snacks in the Korean tempura tradition — fried squid, shrimp, sweet potato, and 김말이 (seaweed-and-noodle rolls) — sold at 분식 stalls beside 떡볶이 and 순대. Because it comes from a verb, the number-one pitfall is mixing up 튀김 (the noun: the fried food) with 튀기다/튀긴 (the verb: to fry / fried), as in 갓 튀긴 튀김 'just-fried fritters', where both appear. A second trap is scope: a bare 튀김 usually implies a mixed assortment (모둠), so to order one specific kind you must name the ingredient — 오징어 튀김, 새우 튀김 — rather than just 튀김. The whole point is 바삭함 (crispiness), best 갓 튀긴 (just fried) and ruined when 눅눅하다 (soggy); dunking them in spicy 떡볶이 국물 is the classic move.

Describing stale fritters with the wrong adjective — lost crunch is 눅눅하다, the opposite of 바삭하다.

usage: Counted by 개; traditionally offered with tea.
Bite-size 미니 약과 became a huge trend snack.
It is honey-soaked; 달다 (sweet) is a ㄹ-final adjective (달아요).
Packaged mini versions sell by the 봉지.
examples: 약과가 겉은 쫀득하고 안은 부드러워요.
Yakgwa is chewy outside and soft inside.
쫀득하다 = pleasantly chewy; -고 links two qualities.
약과는 명절에 차례상에 꼭 올라가는 한과예요.
Yakgwa is a traditional sweet that always goes on the holiday ritual table.
한과 = traditional confection; 차례상 = ancestral-rite table; 올라가다 = to be placed on.
요즘 젊은 사람들 사이에서 약과가 다시 유행이라 카페에서도 약과 디저트를 팔아요.
Yakgwa is trendy again among young people, so cafés even sell yakgwa desserts now.
Part of the 할매니얼 (grandma + millennial) retro-snack craze; -이라 = because it is.
nuance: 약과 is a traditional Korean confection (한과): a wheat-flour dough that is deep-fried and then steeped in honey or grain syrup, historically reserved for holidays and ritual tables. Its 한자 is the key insight — 藥菓, literally 'medicine-confection', because in old Korea honey was considered medicinal (藥 'medicine' is the same character as in 약 'medicine' and 한약 herbal medicine; 菓 'confection' is the same as in 과자). So the standout English-speaker pitfall is assuming the name means it contains medicine: it does not — it is simply a honey cookie whose historical luxury ingredient earned the 'medicine' label. The other boundary to keep straight is 약과 (a specific 한과) vs the broad 과자 (mass-market packaged snacks): 약과 is not a 과자, even though both share the 菓 character. Texture is 쫀득하다 (chewy-sticky) and it is quite sweet (달다). It has surged back into fashion among people in their 20s-30s as part of the 할매니얼 retro-snack trend, with cafés selling 미니 약과 and yakgwa-topped desserts.
